newsitem.title: USA: Enron is joining PJM to supply Amtrak.
newsitem.headline: Enron is joining PJM to supply Amtrak.

text.p: Enron Capital & Trade Resources is in the process of joining the Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Maryland Interconnection Association, according to Director of Power Marketing Don Black.
This is a necessary step before requesting the association, commonly known as PJM, deliver power to Amtrak under the contract announced May 1, he explained.
The Enron Corp subsidiary agreed to provide the electric traction power used on Amtrak's Northeast corridor linking New York City, Harrisburg, Pa., and Washington via Philadelphia.

After reaching agreement with Amtrak, known formally as the National Railroad Passenger Corp, Enron entered into discussion with the PJM, reviewing its tariffs available before requesting transmission of Amtrak's power and ancillary services, Black said in a telephone interview.
He said PJM will not provide ancillary services to non-members, resulting in the decision to join PJM. Enron is already involved "in a lot of trading activity within PJM," he pointed out.
The company expects to submit a request for transmission and ancillary services as early as July 1, he added.

Noting Amtrak's present suppliers -- all PJM members -- consider the railroad a retail purchaser ineligable to make wholesale power purchases, Black said "we wouldn't be surprised" the association rejected the request.

If PJM rejects the request or refuses to act on it for 60 days, Amtrak and Enron will ask the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to declare the railroad is a wholesale power purchaser, Amtrak's Amy Linden told Reuters.
"They take, on average, six to nine months to act" once such a request is filed, she said of FERC.
Under the commission's regulations, she noted, the railroad could not seek designation as a wholesale purchaser until it had a contract to purchase power.
Linden, Amtrak's vice president of business development, Northeast Corridor, said the railroad considered asking Congress to legislate its status as a wholesale buyer.
Instead, she said, it decided to take the regulatory route because Amtrak resells more than half the 600 million kilowatt hours it purchases in an average year to regional commuter railroads.

Currently, Linden said, Amtrak purchases "a little over half" of its power from PECO Energy Co, although it can vary power purchases among its three suppliers -- PECO, PP&L Resources Inc and Baltimore Gas & Electric Co.
The purchases are under monthly, renewable contracts.

The PECO contract has a capacity provision, she said, explaining this means Amtrack's contract with Enron will initially provide savings in the 30 percent range rather than the 50 percent announced May 1.
The contract was the result of Enron's response to Amtrak's RFP -- request for proposal -- to provide its power needs which peak at 250 megawatts, Black said.
None of the utilities serving the areas linked by the Northeast Corridor responded to the RFP, he noted.
When asked why, most of the responses mirrored that of Public Service Enterprise Group Inc spokesman George Koodry: "Amtrak is not a wholesale customer."
When asked why, he responded "...by definition, it is not in our opinion."
But Orange and Rockland Utilities Inc's Mike Donovan said "We receive hundreds (of RFPs) we don't respond to."
Despite PS Enterprise's reluctance, officials of its Energis Resources subsidiary said "We'd be interested (in such RFPs) in the future."
((-- New York Newsdesk 212 859-1610))
